Nob
nob
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Nob (H5011), a town near Jerusalem in the territory of Benjamin; called "the city of the priests" (1 Sam 22:19). The meaning is uncertain, possibly "high place."

See also: Nob

📖 Biblical Definition

Nob was a town near Jerusalem known as "the city of the priests," where the tabernacle and the priesthood resided for a time after the destruction of Shiloh, and which became the scene of a terrible massacre when Saul, in his murderous pursuit of David, slaughtered its priests. When David fled from Saul, he came to Nob to Ahimelech the priest, who, not knowing David was a fugitive, gave him the consecrated shewbread to eat (the only bread at hand) and the sword of Goliath, which had been kept there (1 Sam 21:1-9). The Lord Jesus later cited this incident — David eating the shewbread that was lawful only for the priests — to teach that mercy and necessity may rightly set aside ceremonial restriction, and that "the sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath" (Mark 2:25-27; Matt 12:3-4). But the visit to Nob had a horrifying sequel. Doeg the Edomite, Saul's chief herdsman, had witnessed the priest's kindness to David and reported it. Saul, in a paranoid rage, summoned Ahimelech and the priests of Nob, accused them of conspiracy, and ordered them killed; when his own soldiers refused to lift their hands against the priests of the LORD, Doeg the Edomite fell upon them and slew eighty-five priests in one day, and then put the whole city of Nob to the sword — men, women, children, and cattle (1 Sam 22:9-19). Only Abiathar, a son of Ahimelech, escaped to David. The massacre at Nob is one of the darkest deeds in Saul's tragic decline: a king so consumed by jealousy and rage that he murdered the priests of God and destroyed a whole city of His servants. It fulfilled, in part, the earlier judgment pronounced against the house of Eli (1 Sam 2:31-33), and it stands as a sober monument to the murderous lengths of unchecked jealousy and to the cost borne by the innocent when a ruler casts off the fear of God.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A town near Jerusalem, "the city of the priests," where Ahimelech gave David the shewbread and Goliath's sword (1 Sam 21; cited by the Lord at Mark 2:25-27); later the scene of Saul's massacre of 85 priests and the whole city by Doeg the Edomite (1 Sam 22:9-19); a monument to the cost of unchecked jealousy.

NOB, proper noun. Hebrew Nob (H5011); a town near Jerusalem in Benjamin, "the city of the priests" (1 Sam 22:19).

Where the tabernacle and priesthood resided after Shiloh's destruction; Ahimelech the priest ministered there.

Ahimelech gave the fleeing David the consecrated shewbread and the sword of Goliath (1 Sam 21:1-9).

The Lord Jesus cited this to teach that mercy and necessity may set aside ceremonial restriction (Mark 2:25-27).

Saul had Doeg the Edomite massacre 85 priests and the whole city of Nob (1 Sam 22:9-19); only Abiathar escaped.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Samuel 21:6 — "So the priest gave him hallowed bread: for there was no bread there but the shewbread, that was taken from before the LORD."

1 Samuel 22:18-19 — "And Doeg the Edomite turned, and he fell upon the priests, and slew on that day fourscore and five persons that did wear a linen ephod. And Nob, the city of the priests, smote he with the edge of the sword."

Mark 2:25-26 — "Have ye never read what David did, when he had need, and was an hungred, he, and they that were with him? How he went into the house of God... and did eat the shewbread, which is not lawful to eat but for the priests."

1 Samuel 2:31 — "Behold, the days come, that I will cut off thine arm, and the arm of thy father's house, that there shall not be an old man in thine house."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Nob is corrupted when the shewbread incident is read merely as a rule-breaking precedent, when the massacre is passed over as incidental, or when the lesson about the murderous fruit of unchecked jealousy is softened.

expand to see more

Shewbread-precedent flattened. The Lord Jesus cited David's eating the shewbread at Nob to make a profound point about the law: ceremonial restrictions yield to mercy and genuine need, for "the sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath" (Mark 2:27). This is not a license to break God's law at will, but a principle that the ceremonial law serves human good under God and bends to mercy and necessity (Matt 12:7, "I will have mercy, and not sacrifice"). David, in real need and flight, ate the bread lawful only for priests, and the Lord vindicates him — teaching the Pharisees, who would condemn His disciples for plucking grain on the Sabbath, that they had missed the heart of the law. The Nob incident is a window into how mercy fulfills rather than violates the law's intent.

Nob has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering, beyond the shewbread, is the horror of the massacre and its lesson. Saul, consumed by jealousy of David, slaughtered eighty-five priests of the LORD and a whole city of innocents because one priest had unknowingly aided his rival. His own soldiers refused to raise their hands against the priests; it took the foreign mercenary Doeg the Edomite to do the deed. The massacre at Nob is a monument to the murderous lengths of unchecked jealousy in a ruler who has cast off the fear of God, and to the innocent blood that is shed when power serves paranoia. It is also a fulfillment of God's judgment on the house of Eli (1 Sam 2:31-33), a reminder that the LORD's word against sin, though long delayed, is sure.
